Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book editor who decides to take a non-stop train to Berlin. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his mistress scheming to murder the man's wife (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a bunch of refugees, and even more people. Meant as a mix of noir-ish thriller (which it does quite well - at least to begin with), and comedy, the film fails with both. It doesn't sit right as the film changes tone with every new scene. And as the train races towards its final destination, the film turns more and more bizarre, ending on a truly surreal note. The good bits are wasted in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the performances are just as bad as the script (act your lines - don't read them!). The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pace is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually) with on scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace decent dialogue. The film looks great though, in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other department. [1/10]

"Blue All Fire" is a great song, and the footage of it being performed is probably the best part of the DVD. The interviews, which are not particularly interesting, should have been placed at the end of the DVD, or located as a bonus feature. The best part of concert DVDs is to turn them on and let the music play, but in this DVD, it is next to impossible to stay put and and simply press play because the music is continually interrupted. Nevertheless, there are a few strengths to this DVD; the concert footage, when it does play, is excellent. The band returns to the stage after the end of the song, and the DVD captures that well: it basically shows the fans. The fans, of course, have a sweet advantage in this film because they are seeing the band live, of course, but also they are not forced to deal with the constant interruptions that plague us the DVD viewers..

This film was a good effort on the whole. I can see why George Pal went into Politics if he wanted to. MGM could not have given him the films he wanted. But, as I said earlier. this film was a good effort and a good story. It featured two of my favourite actors from MGM in the 40's--John Payne and Lionel Bogmore(the latter was a bit actor in this film). The music was a bit out of times, but it didn't detract from the the quality of the film. The only reason I gave it 4 stars is because of the fact that it would have been on the B side of the Program when double features were the go.

The problem is the way that is done, without any care, without any taste, just a rumble of bad taste clichés everywhere. The script is so fake and the characters so unreal that's makes petty seeing nice actors as Unas, Bryner, Morgado, Lagarto and others, lost themselves in a net of whatever except cinema or storytelling. For my surprise the newcomers Jorge Corrula and Soraia Chaves bravely stick in their performances, but you can see them lost like a drifted boat without any direction. And talking about direction, this seems to be something totally missing on this movie where's the Director? Everything is bad taste; the frames are whatever, and whenever, the use of hand camera without any justified reason, the light design that should build environments doesn't exist (and no excuses that the all point is a dark real story). It's sad to see Jorge and Soraia melting away in such fake and gratuity sex scenes, painted here and there trough out the movie like closing narratives holes or used as fakes transition motives. Maybe Carlos Coelho da Silva should see the 2002 Carlos Carrera adaptation of the same book of Eça and get the felling of how to build a true movie.

I was limited to my assumptions on the topic, but for sure was a good experience to free myself from the stress of the day and watch a series that gave me a better appreciation of the art form as well as a lot of possible good ideas. I was surprised to see that the series was based on a novel by Carlos M Marquez, and I had been interested in the book, but I was not sure about the quality of the series. I remember seeing nice actors as the characters, such as Bard Cruz, Javier Bardem, and others, but I was not sure about the quality of the series. For my surprise the newcomers Jorge Pera, and Ana García, were bravely good in the roles, and I was eager to continue to watch the rest of the series. I was impressed by the the quality of the series, from the quality of the writing to the quality of the acting; the quality of the directing, the quality of the the lighting, the quality of the music, and the ability to build environments that were immersive and realistic. I am eager to see the the rest of the and I hope will be to watch on Netflix, so that I can continue to appreciate the quality of the series. The chemistry between Jorge and Ana was was melting, and the themes of gratuity and love were painted with care, either in the opening and closing narratives, or in the middle part of the series.. I am eager to see the rest of the series and I hope that the will be to the streaming services, so that I can continue to appreciate the quality of the series.

This frothy romantic comedy is based on a classic short story I loved as a child, and I enjoyed it as an adult. In the case of May-September attachments, doubtless what is on the mind of the elder party is either lust, or a desire to use the younger person as a potential heir. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind parent that he (or she) lacked as a child. So the agendas are more psychological than romantic, and the film does not good job of sorting them out. The younger lover is often innocent and naive--especially if he is seventeen--and the elder lover is wise and sophisticated. I was, however,, put off by the idea of a thirty-year-old romancing a seventeen-year-old. But young Jennifer Roberts is a knockout beauty, and the chemistry is fun. I would have liked to see the seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the morally upright and honest man, or as a subject for a psychological study. This spirited comedy would get from me a better rating than it did at the box. The film was cast well, the beautiful young actress is a real beauty, and the chemistry is fun and infectious. But the writing and direction are not quite there, and the film is not bitty enough bitty. 3/5

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Though a fan of shock and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and puppet work were impressive, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. See, the first act of the film is spent establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the first title cards. As for the narration and many of the flashbacks: needless. The pacing during the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the schlock is punctuated with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the entertaining scenes in the film -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods on without conflict or adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Ash go into production.

I remember when this mini-series was first shown in the U.S. as I was growing up in Australia at the time. Having read the reviews on this title, it must have been very popular with people in Greece as it was produced to coincide with the 1996 Olympics. However, it must have been unpopular with some U.S. viewers due to the fact that the American flag was always in the background and the American athletes were glorified as the gold medal winners. Some of the viewers would have been offended that the fact that the athletes were from the host country was not emphasized. It may, however, help to explain the lack of interest that American spectators showed at the 1996 Olympics. It would suggest that perhaps they were only interested in events that Americans were likely to win.
